item.aggregated_output: {"id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","track":"held_out","category":"functional_inference","prompt":"Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases have related catalytic-domain architecture in SCOPe. What common evolutionary or mechanistic conclusions are justified, and what evidence is needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation?"}

item.text:
{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","answer":"SCOPe places these catalytic domains in the protein kinase-like fold (d.144) and protein kinase-like superfamily (d.144.1), within the alpha+beta class. Their superfamily relationship supports remote common ancestry of the catalytic core. Fold similarity alone would establish shared architecture with weaker evolutionary implications; class membership alone does not establish homology. Distinct families within the superfamily can have substantially different substrates and regulation.

The shared core supports a conserved mechanistic framework: nucleotide binding between two lobes and, in active enzymes, typically divalent-metal-assisted transfer of ATP’s terminal phosphate to a substrate hydroxyl. It does not establish catalytic activity for every member, identical catalytic residues, or identical reaction kinetics.

Canonical protein kinases generally phosphorylate protein serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues. Aminoglycoside phosphotransferases phosphorylate hydroxyl groups on aminoglycosides, often contributing to antibiotic resistance. Phosphoinositide 3-kinases phosphorylate the 3-hydroxyl of the inositol headgroup of phosphoinositides; their preferred lipid substrates differ among PI3K classes. None of these substrate preferences can be transferred across the superfamily merely from structural similarity.

Specificity transfer requires closer sequence and phylogenetic placement, conservation of catalytic and substrate-recognition residues, and preferably substrate-bound structures plus direct biochemical assays comparing plausible substrates and phosphorylation sites. Physiological assignments additionally require evidence of substrate availability, localization, and cellular effects; antibiotic-resistance claims require appropriate susceptibility evidence.

Regulatory transfer requires examination of the complete protein’s domain architecture, regulatory partners, phosphorylation sites, localization signals, and direct functional evidence. Protein-kinase activation-loop or autoinhibitory mechanisms cannot automatically be assigned to aminoglycoside phosphotransferases or PI3Ks, nor can PI3K regulatory-subunit interactions be generalized to all members. A shared-core structural template can support modeling of conserved regions, but substrate-binding loops and regulatory interfaces need closer templates or independent validation. Even same-family membership strengthens rather than guarantees functional transfer.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
